subject: science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The structure and composition of the Earth (crust, mantle, core)
The rock cycle and the three types of rock
The Earth as a source of limited resources and the value of recycling
Human production of carbon dioxide and its impact on climate

questions.lo: The structure and composition of the Earth (crust, mantle, core)
questions.q: Starting from the outside and going inwards, what is the correct order of the Earth's main layers?
questions.explain: From the outside in the Earth has a thin solid crust, then a thick mantle, then the core at the centre.

questions.lo: The structure and composition of the Earth (crust, mantle, core)
questions.q: The Earth's core is mostly made of which materials?
questions.explain: The core is mainly iron and nickel. It is the hottest part of the Earth and lies at the very centre.

questions.lo: The structure and composition of the Earth (crust, mantle, core)
questions.q: Which statement about the Earth's layers is correct?
options: The crust is the thickest layer
The mantle is the thickest layer
The core is thinner than the crust
All three layers are the same thickness
questions.explain: The mantle is by far the thickest layer. The crust is very thin compared with the mantle and core.

questions.q: Which gas makes up the largest part of the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air. It is a common mistake to think air is mostly oxygen — oxygen is only about 21%.

questions.q: About what percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?
questions.explain: Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of the air. Nitrogen is about 78% and the remaining ~1% is other gases such as argon and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: The 'other gases' that make up roughly 1% of the atmosphere are mostly which gas?
questions.explain: The remaining ~1% of the air is mostly argon, along with a small amount of carbon dioxide and other trace gases.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the three types of rock
options: Layers of sediment are squashed together
An existing rock is changed by heat and pressure
questions.explain: Igneous rock forms when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies. Granite and basalt are examples.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the three types of rock
questions.q: Which type of rock forms when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting?
questions.explain: Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock. 'Meta' means changed — for example marble forms from limestone.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the three types of rock
questions.q: A rock is found in flat layers and contains fossils. Which type of rock is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: Layers and fossils are typical of sedimentary rock, which forms as sediments and remains settle, are buried and cemented together.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the three types of rock
questions.q: Which statement about the rock cycle is correct?
options: Once a rock is igneous it can never change type
Over very long times, any rock can be turned into a different type
Only sedimentary rock can change type
Rocks change type every few days
questions.explain: In the rock cycle, given enough time and the right conditions, any rock can be changed into another type. A rock's type is not fixed forever.

questions.lo: The Earth as a source of limited resources and the value of recycling
questions.q: Why do we describe most metals and fossil fuels from the Earth as 'limited' resources?
options: They are made fresh every day
Once used up they are gone or take millions of years to replace
There is an endless supply of them
questions.explain: These resources are non-renewable — once extracted and used they are gone, or take millions of years to form again, so supplies are limited.

questions.lo: The Earth as a source of limited resources and the value of recycling
questions.q: Which is the best reason recycling aluminium is good for the environment?
options: It uses no energy at all
It uses less energy and less ore, so limited metal lasts longer
It turns aluminium into a renewable resource
It removes carbon dioxide from the air
questions.explain: Recycling aluminium uses far less energy and less ore than extracting new metal, helping conserve a limited resource. Recycling still uses some energy — it is not free.

questions.lo: The Earth as a source of limited resources and the value of recycling
questions.q: Which statement about recycling is most accurate?
options: Recycling makes materials without using any energy
Recycling saves resources but still needs energy to collect, sort and process materials
Everything can be recycled endlessly with no problems
questions.explain: Recycling saves raw materials and usually energy, but it still needs energy to collect, clean, sort and process materials — and some materials are hard to recycle.

questions.q: Which process takes carbon dioxide OUT of the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis in green plants removes carbon dioxide from the air. Respiration and burning (combustion) both release carbon dioxide back into the air.

questions.q: Which two processes RELEASE carbon dioxide into the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Respiration by living things and combustion (burning fuels) both release carbon dioxide, while photosynthesis takes it back in.

questions.q: In the natural carbon cycle, how does the carbon dioxide removed by plants compare with the carbon dioxide put back?
options: Much more is removed than put back
Much more is put back than removed
questions.explain: Naturally the carbon cycle stays roughly balanced — the CO2 taken out by photosynthesis is about equal to the CO2 returned by respiration and combustion.

questions.lo: Human production of carbon dioxide and its impact on climate
questions.q: Which human activity adds the most extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
options: Burning fossil fuels for energy and transport
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) releases large amounts of carbon dioxide that had been locked underground, making it the main human cause of rising CO2.

questions.lo: Human production of carbon dioxide and its impact on climate
questions.q: How does extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere lead to climate change?
options: It makes a hole that lets more Sun through
It traps more of the Earth's heat, raising average temperatures
It cools the Earth by blocking sunlight
It has no effect on temperature
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide traps heat like a blanket. More CO2 means more heat is trapped, raising average temperatures — this is climate change. CO2 does not make a hole or burn the Earth.

questions.lo: Human production of carbon dioxide and its impact on climate
questions.q: Besides burning fossil fuels, which activity also increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?
options: Cutting down large areas of forest
questions.explain: Cutting down forests (deforestation) means fewer trees to take in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, so more CO2 stays in the atmosphere.

specSource: National Curriculum in England: science programme of study, Key Stage 3; Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere
